title: Voxel-scale tracer projection density does not predict short-latency spike links between mouse visual areas better than distance in two Allen Neuropixels datasets
abstract:
Question: does the point-to-point axon density between two positions in mouse visual cortex, predicted from Allen anterograde tracer data, tell which cross-area unit pairs have a short-latency directed spike link?

Approach: We made a 100 um flatmap kernel-regression model of visual-cortex projections from 289 Allen tracer injections (leave-one-out r of log density 0.88 at a 200 um kernel; 0.63 without position). For each directed cross-correlogram test between units in two of six visual areas, the model gave the predicted density D from the source unit position at the target unit position. Data: Allen Visual Coding Neuropixels (passive; 3.37 million tests, 5,921 links, 50 mice) and Allen Visual Behavior Neuropixels (task; 4.84 million tests, 33,831 links, 34 mice). We used Poisson models with absorbed fixed effects and mouse-clustered errors.

Result: Without a distance control, D predicted links in Visual Coding (rate ratio 2.18 per 10-fold D, z = 4.97). A spline of inter-unit distance removed most of this association (1.22, 95% CI 0.92-1.62). In Visual Behavior, D had no association at any level of adjustment (main model 0.94, 0.77-1.16). Distance alone was a strong predictor in both datasets: the link rate at 3 mm was 0.19 and 0.13 of the rate at 0.5 mm. In five variants (strict links, wild-type tracers, kernels of 100 and 400 um), Visual Coding estimates were always above 1 (3 of 10 significant) and Visual Behavior estimates were always below 1. No pooled estimate differed from 1. The reverse-direction density was not a better predictor.

Limitation: D is a model prediction at tracer resolution (injections of about 0.5-1 mm) from other animals. Probe placement limits the range of D. A CCG link is not proof of a monosynaptic connection.
